overview.title: 📖 Overview: Coals, Water Temperature, and Set-Aside Vessels
overview.subtitle: Shabbat 42a–42b
overview.hebrewSource: הָאִילְפָּס וְהַקְּדֵרָה שֶׁהֶעֱבִירָן מְרוּתָּחִין — לֹא יִתֵּן לְתוֹכָן תַּבְלִין
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: The daf opens by analyzing Shmuel's ruling that one may extinguish a white-hot metal coal in a public area to prevent injury, asking whether this fits Rabbi Shimon's view that an unintended prohibited labor is permitted. The Gemara distinguishes unintentional acts from labor not needed for its own sake, then moves to a baraita on pouring hot and cold water together, where Beit Shammai, Beit Hillel, and Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya disagree, and the halakha is fixed like the latter. A new mishna then forbids adding spices to a boiling pot removed from the fire, sparking a dispute over whether Rabbi Yehuda is lenient or strict, and whether salt behaves like a spice. The daf closes with a mishna forbidding a vessel placed to catch lamp oil, which leads into Rav Chisda's ruling about receiving a hen's egg.

slides.title: 🔥 Why May One Extinguish a Dangerous Coal?
slides.subtitle: The Gemara tests Shmuel's ruling against Rabbi Shimon's principle

nodes.content: ❓ Shmuel permits extinguishing a white-hot metal coal in public so people won't be hurt, but not a wood coal. Does this mean Shmuel rules like Rabbi Shimon, who exempts a labor not needed for its own sake?
🚫 If so, wood should also be permitted — extinguishing it too is a labor not needed for its own sake, just to prevent injury

columns.label: Unintentional act
columns.content: Shmuel agrees with Rabbi Shimon: no intent to do the prohibited labor at all, so it is permitted

columns.label: Labor not for its own sake
columns.content: Shmuel holds like Rabbi Yehuda: liable, since extinguishing a wood coal is Torah-level and metal is only rabbinic

nodes.content: ✅ Ravina: therefore a thorn in the public domain may be carried less than four cubits at a time; in a karmelit, even more

callout.label: Key distinction:
callout.text: A white-hot metal coal is not yet 'fire' by Torah law, so extinguishing it is only rabbinic; the Sages did not decree where public safety is at stake.

slides.title: 🌡️ Pouring Hot and Cold Water Together
slides.subtitle: A baraita records three positions, and Rav Nachman rules like the last

callout.label: Halakha:
callout.text: Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya. He is explained as referring only to Beit Hillel's first clause, meaning Beit Shammai and Beit Hillel never truly disagreed on this point.

slides.title: 🛁 Is a Wash-Basin Like a Bathtub?
slides.subtitle: Rav Yosef's assumption is corrected, then the Gemara worries it removes all hot washing on Shabbat

lines.speaker: Rav Yosef
lines.text: I would say a סֵפֶל (basin) has the same status as an אַמְבָּטִי (bath) — cold may not be poured into it.

lines.speaker: Abaye
lines.text: Rabbi Ḥiyya taught: a basin is not like a bath.

lines.speaker: Gemara
lines.text: But if a basin really were like a bath, and the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya who forbids cold into hot even for a bath — would that mean there is no way at all to wash with hot water on Shabbat?

lines.speaker: Answer
lines.text: No such sweeping prohibition was ever taught. Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya's stringency addresses only the first clause of the baraita, about hot into cold — not all washing.

callout.label: Result:
callout.text: A basin retains the lenient status of a cup, not the stringent status of a bath.

slides.title: 🍲 Spices Into a Boiling Pot: Lenient or Strict?
slides.subtitle: The mishna forbids seasoning a still-hot pot; Rabbi Yehuda's exception is ambiguous

boxes.title: First Clause: Lenient?
items: Mishna forbids spices into any boiling pot
Rabbi Yehuda might loosen this: only pots with vinegar or brine are forbidden

boxes.title: Second Clause: Strict?
items: Rabbi Yehuda allows spices into a bowl or tureen (secondary vessel)
He might add a stringency there: except one with vinegar or brine

boxes.title: Resolution
items: Baraita: 'into all stew pots, into all boiling pots' one may place spices, except vinegar or brine
Proves Rabbi Yehuda is lenient on the first clause

callout.label: Come and hear:
callout.text: The explicit baraita settles the dilemma raised before the Sages in favor of the lenient reading.

slides.title: 🪔 From Lamp Oil to a Hen's Egg
slides.subtitle: The mishna's oil ruling and Rav Chisda's parallel about eggs

steps.content: 1️⃣ Mishna: one may not place a vessel beneath the oil lamp to catch dripping oil; if placed before Shabbat, the vessel is fine but the oil is unusable — it was never prepared for Shabbat use
2️⃣ Rav Chisda: though one may not place a vessel to catch a hen's egg as it is laid, one may overturn a vessel onto the egg so it won't break
3️⃣ Rabba explains why: a hen usually lays in a garbage dump (common risk of breakage) rather than on a slope (uncommon risk) — the Sages permitted acting only for common cases of preservation

4️⃣ Abaye objects twice: a barrel of untithed produce that breaks on the roof may be caught (even though uncommon), and a vessel may catch sparks from a lamp — both answered as themselves 'common' cases (new barrels break often; sparks are frequent)

callout.label: Salt vs. spice (bonus dispute):
callout.text: Rav Yosef and Abaye also debate, in two conflicting versions, whether salt cooks in a primary vessel the way a spice does — tied to Rav Naḥman's rule that salt needs as much cooking as ox meat.

summary.principle: Shmuel distinguishes unintentional acts (always permitted) from labor not needed for its own sake (a Torah-level dispute), and this same care for precise categories runs through the daf's rulings on water temperature, seasoning a hot pot, and protecting a vessel's usability on Shabbat.

flowSteps.content: 🔥 Extinguishing a dangerous coal: unintentional (permitted) vs. labor not for its own sake (disputed)
🌡️ Hot/cold water: halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya — no cold into a hot bath

columns.content: 🍲 Rabbi Yehuda is lenient: only vinegar/brine pots stay forbidden
🪔 A vessel may be moved only for a common case of preservation

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: Shabbat's set-aside and cooking rules turn on intent, frequency, and the vessel's original designation

quiz.q: Why does Shmuel permit extinguishing a white-hot metal coal in public but not a wood coal?
o: Metal coals are not dangerous
Extinguishing metal is only a rabbinic prohibition since it isn't yet 'fire' by Torah law, and the Sages didn't decree where public safety is at stake
Wood coals cannot injure people
Metal coals extinguish themselves
quiz.e: A white-hot metal coal is not actual fire, so extinguishing it violates only a rabbinic decree, which the Sages waived for public safety; a wood coal's extinguishing is Torah-level.

quiz.q: According to the halakha as Rav Nachman rules, may one pour cold water into a large amount of hot water (a bath) on Shabbat?
o: Yes, always permitted
No — the halakha follows Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who forbids cold into hot
Only if done before Shabbat
Only in a cup, never a bath
quiz.e: Rav Nachman rules like Rabbi Shimon ben Menasya, who prohibits pouring cold water into hot water, understood as addressing Beit Hillel's leniency in the mishna's first clause.

quiz.q: How does the Gemara resolve whether a sefel (basin) has the status of an ambatti (bath) for pouring water?
o: A basin is always treated like a bath
Rabbi Ḥiyya taught that a basin is not like a bath — it keeps the lenient status of a cup
Baskets may never hold water on Shabbat
The question is left unresolved (teiku)
quiz.e: Abaye cites Rabbi Ḥiyya's teaching that a basin is not comparable to a bath, so the stricter rule for baths does not apply to it.

quiz.q: What does the explicit baraita prove about Rabbi Yehuda's ruling on spices and a boiling pot?
o: He is stringent on the mishna's second clause about bowls
He is lenient on the first clause — only pots containing vinegar or brine remain forbidden
He forbids spices in every vessel
He only discusses cold pots
quiz.e: The baraita states that into all stew pots and all boiling pots one may place spices except where there is vinegar or brine, proving Rabbi Yehuda is lenient regarding the mishna's first clause.

quiz.q: Why does Rabba permit overturning a vessel onto a hen's egg to protect it, but not placing a vessel beneath the hen to catch the egg as it's laid?
o: Eggs laid on a slope are a common case worth protecting against, but a vessel is not moved for the uncommon act of catching a falling egg
Hens on Shabbat may not lay eggs at all
A hen typically lays in a garbage dump where breakage is common, but landing on a slope where it could roll and break is uncommon, and one may only act for a common case of preservation
Both actions are actually forbidden
quiz.e: Rabba explains that Rav Chisda's leniency applies only to preserving against a common mishap (breaking in a dump); catching an egg mid-fall to prevent an uncommon mishap (rolling down a slope) was not permitted.
